rows.stem: Which one of the following has half the number of chromosomes and half the amount of DNA as compared to the non-reproductive body cells?

options.label: D
options.text: Both, male and female germ cells

rows.solution:
Germ cells are made by a special kind of division that halves the chromosome number, so each germ cell, male or female, carries one set of chromosomes and half the DNA of a body cell. The zygote, formed when the two fuse, gets back the full number.

This is option (D) Both, male and female germ cells.

rows.stem:
**Assertion (A) :** All exothermic reactions are accompanied with evolution of heat and light.

**Reason (R) :** Combination reactions may or may not be exothermic.
rows.context: Question Nos. 17 to 20 consist of two statements – Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Answer these questions selecting the appropriate option (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both, Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is **not** the correct explanation of Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
An exothermic reaction is one in which heat is released; light need not be given out. Respiration and the reaction of quicklime with water release heat without any light. So the Assertion is false.

Most combination reactions release heat, but some absorb it (nitrogen and oxygen combine to form nitric oxide only on absorbing heat). So combination reactions may or may not be exothermic, and the Reason is true.

So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true, which is option (D) Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.stem: While burning a magnesium ribbon in air, list two safety measures which should be followed. Also state two observations of this activity.
rows.solution:
Safety measures:

1. Hold the magnesium ribbon with a pair of tongs, not with the fingers.

2. Burn the ribbon keeping it as far as possible from the eyes, or wear protective glasses, because the dazzling light can harm the eyes.

Observations:

1. The ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame.

2. It changes into a white powder (ash), which is magnesium oxide:

\(\mathrm{2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO}\)

rows.stem: “In human alimentary canal the small intestine is designed to absorb the digested food.” Justify this statement.
rows.solution:
The inner lining of the small intestine has numerous finger-like projections called villi. They greatly increase the surface area available for absorbing the digested food.

The villi are richly supplied with blood vessels, which take up the absorbed food and carry it to each and every cell of the body. The small intestine is also very long, so the food stays in it long enough to be absorbed.

rows.stem:
Pure-tall (TT) pea plants are crossed with pure-dwarf (tt) pea plants. The pea plants obtained in \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation are then self pollinated to produce \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation.

(i) What do the plants of \(\mathrm{F_1}\) generation look-like? Justify your answer.

(ii) What is the ratio of pure-tall plants to pure-dwarf plants in \(\mathrm{F_2}\) generation ?
rows.solution:
(i) A pure-tall plant gives only T gametes and a pure-dwarf plant only t gametes, so every \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plant is Tt. All the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants are tall, because tallness is the dominant trait: a single T is enough to make the plant tall, and the recessive t does not show.

(ii) Selfing the \(\mathrm{F_1}\) plants: Tt \(\times\) Tt. Each parent gives T and t gametes in equal numbers, so the \(\mathrm{F_2}\) plants are

TT : Tt : tt = 1 : 2 : 1

The pure-tall plants (TT) are one quarter and the pure-dwarf plants (tt) are one quarter, so the ratio of pure-tall to pure-dwarf plants is 1 : 1.

rows.stem: State the role of an electric fuse, used in series with an electrical appliance. Why should in an electric circuit a fuse with defined rating not be replaced by one with a larger rating?
rows.solution:
An electric fuse is a safety device. It protects the appliance and the circuit from damage due to short-circuiting or overloading: when the current exceeds its rated value, the fuse wire heats up, melts and breaks the circuit.

A fuse of larger rating would not melt at the current the circuit is meant to stop. During short-circuiting or overloading an unduly high current would then keep flowing, and the appliance would be damaged (the wiring could even overheat and catch fire).

rows.stem:
Samples of four metals A, B, C and D were added one by one to the following solutions. The results obtained were tabulated as follows :

| Metal / Solution | Iron Sulphate | Copper Sulphate | Zinc Sulphate | Aluminium Sulphate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | – | Displacement | No reaction | No reaction |
| B | Displacement | Displacement | Displacement | – |
| C | Displacement | ? | – | No reaction |
| D | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction | No reaction |

Use the table above to answer the following questions about metals A, B, C and D :

(i) Which is the least reactive metal?

(ii) What would be observed if C is added to a solution of copper sulphate?

(iii) Arrange the metals A, B, C and D in the order of their decreasing reactivity.
rows.solution:
A dash in the table marks a metal placed in a solution of its own salt, so B is aluminium, C is zinc and A is iron. The reactions show the same order: a metal displaces only the metals less reactive than itself.

(i) D displaces none of the four metals, so D is the least reactive metal.

(ii) C displaces iron from iron sulphate, so it is more reactive than iron and therefore more reactive than copper. It displaces copper from copper sulphate: the blue colour of the solution fades and disappears, and a reddish-brown coating of copper forms on C.

(iii) B displaces iron, copper and zinc; C displaces iron but not aluminium; A displaces only copper; D displaces nothing. In decreasing order of reactivity:

B > C > A > D

rows.stem:
(i) Study the diagram and name the parts marked as A, B, C and D.

(ii) Write the function of A and C.
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED - a schematic of the human double circulation (heart with the lung capillary bed above and the body capillary bed below) with four vessels pointed to by arrows labelled A, B, C and D; which vessel each letter marks is given only in the drawing. Page idx 14.
rows.solution:
(i) In the figure, A is the vessel taking blood from the heart to the lungs, B brings blood back from the lungs to the heart, C carries blood from the heart down to the body, and D returns blood from the body to the heart. So:

A: pulmonary artery

B: pulmonary vein

C: aorta

D: vena cava

(ii) A, the pulmonary artery, carries deoxygenated blood from the heart (right ventricle) to the lungs.

C, the aorta, carries oxygenated blood from the heart (left ventricle) to all parts of the body.

rows.stem: If we want to obtain a real and magnified image of an object by using a concave mirror of focal length 18 cm. Where should the object be placed? Use mirror formula to determine the object distance for an image of magnification \(-2\) by this mirror to justify your answer.
rows.solution:
A concave mirror forms a real, magnified image when the object is placed between the centre of curvature C and the focus F, that is, between 18 cm and 36 cm from the mirror.

Check with the mirror formula, taking \(f = -18\) cm and, for a real inverted image, \(m = -2\):

\(m = -\dfrac{v}{u} = -2\), so \(v = 2u\).

\(\dfrac{1}{v} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}\): \(\dfrac{1}{2u} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{3}{2u} = -\dfrac{1}{18}\), so \(u = -27\) cm.

The object is 27 cm in front of the mirror (and the image forms at \(v = -54\) cm). This lies between F and C, as stated.

rows.stem:
(i) What are structural isomers ? Draw structural isomers of butane \((\mathrm{C_4H_{10}})\). Give reason why propane has no structural isomers ?

(ii) What happens when butane is burnt in air ? Write chemical equation for the reaction. Differentiate between the flames obtained when butane and butyne both are burnt in air in the similar conditions.
rows.solution:
(i) Structural isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures.

Butane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\), has two structural isomers:

1. A straight chain of four carbons, n-butane: \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\)

2. A chain of three carbons with the fourth carbon joined to the middle one as a branch, isobutane: \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(CH_3){-}CH_3}\)

(In the full structures every carbon is shown with its hydrogen atoms so that each carbon has four bonds.)

Propane has only three carbon atoms. They can only be joined in one chain, since attaching the third carbon to the middle one gives the same chain again. No branching is possible, so two different structures cannot be drawn and propane has no structural isomers.

(ii) Butane burns in air to give carbon dioxide and water, with a lot of heat and light:

\(\mathrm{2C_4H_{10} + 13O_2 \rightarrow 8CO_2 + 10H_2O}\) + heat and light

Butane is saturated, so it burns with a clean blue flame. Butyne is unsaturated, so it burns with a yellow, sooty (smoky) flame.

rows.stem:
(i) Give reason why carbon can neither form \(\mathrm{C^{4+}}\) cations nor \(\mathrm{C^{4-}}\) anions but forms covalent compounds.

(ii) What is meant by functional group in carbon compounds ? Write in tabular form the structural formula and the functional group present in the following compounds :

(a) Ethanol

(b) Ethanoic acid
rows.solution:
(i) Carbon (2, 4) has four valence electrons.

It could gain four electrons to form the \(\mathrm{C^{4-}}\) anion, but it would be difficult for a nucleus with six protons to hold on to ten electrons.

It could lose four electrons to form the \(\mathrm{C^{4+}}\) cation, but that would need a large amount of energy, leaving a cation with six protons holding only two electrons.

So carbon shares its valence electrons with other atoms and forms covalent compounds.

(ii) A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms (such as oxygen or a halogen, called heteroatoms) that gives an organic compound its characteristic chemical properties, whatever the length of the carbon chain.

| Compound | Structural formula | Functional group |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Ethanol | \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH_2{-}OH}\) | \(\mathrm{{-}OH}\), alcohol |
| (b) Ethanoic acid | \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}C({=}O){-}OH}\) | \(\mathrm{{-}COOH}\), carboxylic acid |

(In the full structural formulas, all the hydrogen atoms on each carbon are drawn with single bonds, and in ethanoic acid the second carbon carries a double-bonded oxygen and an OH group.)
